questions.text: Which of the following is/are undecidable?
questions.solution:
Options 1-3 ask about a non-trivial property of the language of a TM (equality, regularity, accepting everything). By Rice's theorem they are undecidable.

Option 4 is decidable: in 1073 steps a TM can read at most the first 1073 input symbols, so it is enough to simulate M for 1073 steps on the finitely many strings of length up to 1073.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Given two Turing machines M1 and M2 , decide if L(M1 ) = L(M2 ).
Given a Turing machine M , decide if L(M ) is regular.
Given a Turing machine M , decide if M accepts all strings.
Given a Turing machine M , decide if M takes more than 1073 steps on every string.

questions.text: Consider a simple undirected weighted graph G, all of whose edge weights are distinct. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees of G is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
With distinct weights the MST is unique (so option 4 is false).

- The two smallest edges cannot form a cycle, so Kruskal always takes both [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- If the 3rd smallest is rejected, it closes a triangle with the two smallest edges. Then the 4th edge cannot form a cycle with them (the triangle's 3 vertices are already fully joined), so it is taken [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- This is the cut property: the lightest edge crossing any cut is in every MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The edge with the second smallest weight is always part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
One or both of the edges with the third smallest and the fourth smallest weights are part of any minimum spanning tree of G .

Suppose [latex]S\subseteq V[/latex] be such that [latex]S\neq  \phi [/latex] and [latex]S\neq  V[/latex] . Consider the edge with the minimum weight such that one of its vertices is in S and the other in V \ S . Such an edge will always be part of any minimum spanning tree of G .
G can have multiple minimum spanning trees.

questions.text:
The following simple undirected graph is referred to as the Peterson graph.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Petersen graph: 10 vertices, 3-regular, no triangles or 4-cycles.

- Odd cycles (5-cycles) need 3 colours, and 3 are enough [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] chromatic number 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- It has no Hamiltonian cycle, but it does have a Hamiltonian path (outer cycle 4 vertices, then into the star) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The given graph is also 3-regular on 10 vertices with girth 5, and is a known drawing of the Petersen graph [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- The largest independent set has size 4, not 3 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The chromatic number of the graph is 3.
The graph has a Hamiltonian path.
The following graph is isomorphic to the Peterson graph.
The size of the largest independent set of the given graph is 3. (A subset of vertices of a graph form an independent set if no two vertices of the subset are adjacent.)
